lead: A bent beam stores energy, like a stretched bow. Write that energy in terms of the applied loads and one derivative hands you the deflection under the load. That is Castigliano's theorem. Its companion, Maxwell's reciprocal theorem, says two cross-deflections of the same beam are equal: the deflection at A due to a unit load at B equals the deflection at B due to a unit load at A. Energy methods are the quick route for determinate beams and the standard route for statically indeterminate ones, where double integration becomes heavy.
prereq: You need: strain energy under axial load (see Unit 1, Strain energy under gradual, sudden and impact loads), the bending equation and flexural rigidity EI (see Unit 4, Theory of simple bending and bending equation), and the elastic curve (see 5.1).

sections.h3: Strain energy stored in a bent beam

blocks.text: When a beam bends, fibres on one side stretch and fibres on the other side shorten. The work done by the external loads against this elastic resistance is stored in the beam and is recovered when the loads are removed. That stored work is the strain energy U, measured in joules (J) or, in beam work, in kN·m.

For a small slice of beam of length dx, the bending moment M(x) acts through the curvature it produces. The energy in that slice works out to M(x)² dx / (2EI). Adding all slices gives the strain energy of the whole beam.

blocks.where: U is the strain energy (N·m or kN·m); M(x) is the bending moment at section x (N·m or kN·m); E is Young's modulus (N/m²); I is the second moment of area about the bending axis (m⁴); EI is the flexural rigidity (N·m²); L is the beam length (m).

blocks.text: For pure bending, M is constant over the length, so the integral collapses to U = M²L / (2EI). For anything else you must write M as a function of x and integrate. Use the magnitude of M: it is squared, so a sagging or hogging sign disappears.

The attraction of energy is that it is a scalar. You do not chase slopes or boundary constants. A Chennai workshop checking a canopy beam can square the moment diagram, integrate to get U, then differentiate with respect to the load to read the deflection.

Castigliano's theorem for bending says: the partial derivative of the strain energy with respect to a load gives the displacement of the point where that load acts, measured in the direction of the load.

blocks.where: U is the total strain energy (kN·m); P is the applied load (kN); Δ is the deflection under P in the direction of P (m). A positive result means the deflection is in the same sense as P.

items: Keep the load as a symbol P and write M(x) with P still inside it.
Form U = ∫ M(x)² / (2EI) dx and simplify to a function of P.
Differentiate U with respect to P. Only now put in the number for P.
Check the answer against a standard case such as PL³/(3EI) for a cantilever.

blocks.text: The order matters. If you substitute the numeric P into U first, U becomes a constant and the derivative is zero. The chapter trap is exactly this.

If you want the deflection at a point where no load acts, apply a dummy unit load there, differentiate, then set the dummy to zero. That is the unit load method: Δ = ∫ M m / (EI) dx, where m is the bending moment caused by the unit load alone. It is the same idea dressed for a point of your choosing, and it saves you from inventing a real load.

The double integration method of 5.2 gives the whole elastic curve; Castigliano gives one deflection with less algebra. When several loads act, superpose their M diagrams first, then square (see 5.6).

sections.h3: Maxwell's reciprocal theorem and Betti's theorem

blocks.text: Maxwell's reciprocal theorem states that for a linear elastic beam, the deflection at point A due to a unit load at point B equals the deflection at point B due to a unit load at A. In symbols, δ_AB = δ_BA, where δ_AB means the deflection at A caused by a unit load at B.

The general form is Betti's theorem: the work done by a first system of loads moving through the displacements produced by a second system equals the work done by the second system moving through the displacements of the first. Maxwell's theorem is the special case where each system is a single unit load.

Use it as a free check or a shortcut. A simply supported beam with a unit load at midspan deflects the quarter point by an amount; put the unit load at the quarter point and the midspan deflects by the same amount. Standard deflection tables therefore carry twice the information they appear to.

The theorem is also the reason a flexibility matrix of a beam is symmetric, with the term in row A, column B equal to the term in row B, column A. That symmetry halves the number of flexibility coefficients you must compute by hand, which is why the one-redundancy unit-load equation for a propped cantilever or a fixed beam is so quick to set up (see 5.8).

items: Castigliano: differentiate energy with respect to a load to get deflection.
Unit load method: same derivative with a dummy unit load, then set it to zero.
Maxwell: two reciprocal deflections are equal.
Betti: work of one load system on the other's displacements is symmetric.

figure.caption: Load makes a bending moment; the squared moment integrated over the beam is the strain energy, and its derivative with respect to the load gives the deflection under that load.

spec.title: Energy route to deflection
spec.aria: A block diagram shows load giving bending moment, then strain energy, whose partial derivative gives deflection.

examples.question: A cantilever of length 2 m carries a point load of 6 kN at its free end. EI = 3000 kN·m². Use Castigliano's theorem to find the free-end deflection.
steps: Measure x from the free end. At distance x the bending moment magnitude is M(x) = P x, with P kept as a symbol for now.
Write the energy: U = ∫₀² (P x)² / (2EI) dx = P² / (2EI) × [x³/3]₀² = P² × 8 / (6EI) = 4P² / (3EI).
Convert to millimetres: 0.005333 m × 1000 = 5.333 mm. The sign is positive, so the deflection is downward, the same sense as P.
Check with the standard cantilever result PL³/(3EI) = 6 × 2³ / (3 × 3000) = 48/9000 = 0.005333 m. Same value.
examples.answer: The free-end deflection is 5.333 mm downward.

traps: Differentiating after putting the numeric value of P into U. U then has no P in it and the derivative is zero; keep P symbolic until the derivative is done.
Dropping the factor 2 in the denominator of U = ∫M²/(2EI)dx and using M²/(EI); the energy doubles, so every deflection then comes out twice as large.
Forgetting to square M, or squaring only part of it when two loads act; square the total moment after superposition.
Confusing Castigliano's theorem (derivative with respect to a load) with Maxwell's theorem (equality of two reciprocal deflections). They answer different questions.
Losing units: with P in kN and EI in kN·m², the derivative is in metres, not millimetres; convert at the end.

quiz.q: State Castigliano's theorem for a beam in bending.
quiz.a: The partial derivative of the total strain energy with respect to an applied load equals the deflection of the point of application in the direction of that load: ∂U/∂P = Δ.

quiz.q: Write the expression for strain energy in a beam with a varying bending moment.
quiz.a: U = ∫₀ᴸ M(x)²/(2EI) dx, where M(x) is the bending moment at section x, E is Young's modulus, I is the second moment of area and L is the beam length.

quiz.q: Why must the load P be kept as a symbol while forming and differentiating U?
quiz.a: The theorem differentiates U with respect to P. If the number for P is substituted first, U becomes a constant and ∂U/∂P is zero. Keeping P symbolic keeps the dependence visible, so the derivative gives the correct deflection.

quiz.q: A cantilever of length 3 m carries 4 kN at its free end. EI = 2000 kN·m². Find the free-end deflection using Castigliano's theorem.
A simply supported beam of length L carries a central point load P. Show by Castigliano's theorem that the central deflection is PL³/(48EI).
quiz.a: For 0 ≤ x ≤ L/2, M = Px/2. By symmetry U = 2∫₀^(L/2) (Px/2)²/(2EI) dx = P²L³/(96EI). Then ∂U/∂P = 2PL³/(96EI) = PL³/(48EI) downward.

quiz.q: A unit load at midspan of a simply supported beam deflects the quarter point by δ. What is the midspan deflection when the same unit load acts at the quarter point? Justify.
quiz.a: It is δ, by Maxwell's reciprocal theorem: the deflection at A due to a unit load at B equals the deflection at B due to a unit load at A. Take A as the quarter point and B as midspan.

quiz.q: Two students find the same beam deflection. One differentiates U after substituting P = 6 kN and gets zero; the other gets a finite value. Explain the difference and state who is right.
quiz.a: The first student made U a constant by substituting P first, so ∂U/∂P = 0 is meaningless. The second kept P symbolic, differentiated, then substituted, which is the correct order in Castigliano's theorem. The second student is right.

beyond: Not for the exam. The symmetry that Maxwell's theorem gives a flexibility matrix is the same symmetry seen in the stiffness matrix of every finite element beam model, and commercial structural analysis software relies on it to save half the storage and computation. Energy methods also extend to frames, arches and plates, where the moment integral becomes a volume integral of ½ × stress × strain, U = ∫ ½σε dV. Search next for 'Betti's theorem structural analysis', 'unit load method frames' and 'flexibility matrix symmetry' if you want to see the same ideas at a larger scale.
